items.title: This 'fix' wouldn't have saved F1's Spanish GP
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
The failure of the Spanish Grand Prix to produce the kind of spectacle offered by other Formula 1 races this year has inevitably focused on the lack of overtaking opportunities around the Madring circuit.

Combined entries, barrier pinch points and a lack of wide, heavy braking zones - especially at Turn 5 - all contributed to making it extremely difficult to pass a rival.

It is little wonder, as The Race revealed on Sunday, that Madring chiefs are already planning changes to three key corners for 2027 with the expectation that next year's race produces a bit more of a show.

But it was not just the track layout that contributed to a lack of action, as another factor in how things played out was that there was not much strategic variation either.

Even the most boring of track layouts can deliver thrillers if tyre strategy gets blown open.

Make the fastest route to the chequered flag unclear and you get teams taking different approaches, plus the kinds of pace offset that create the circumstances for wheel-to-wheel action.

The hard tyre's durability

The Madring delivered one of those Monaco/Sochi-style phenomena where the hard tyre (the C2 compound in Spain) was good enough to last the whole race - as Pierre Gasly proved by waiting until the penultimate lap for his mandatory compound switch to get off what he had started the race with.

After tongue-in-cheek claims after first running on Friday of a potential six-stopper being on the cards, based on the high levels of degradation seen, the transformation into an easy one-stopper was remarkable.

Haas driver Esteban Ocon said the behaviour of the tyres was one of the limiting factors in why there was not much action in the race, because drivers could push on without fear of excessive degradation as long as they did not spend too much time in the dirty air of the car ahead.

"The thing is that it was so consistent, the tyres on the second stint, that as soon as you were following another car, you were losing so much grip," he said.

"When I was doing blue flags to other cars, I was losing half a second, seven tenths easily. And then after it was coming back because it was all about overheating.

"As soon as the overheating was coming down, you had pace again. So that's why there was no overtaking. It was too fast, the pace, basically.

"It was like 120% from as soon as you pitted to the end. And because the graining didn't happen, that's where we ended up. If we had a race on Friday, it would have been much better!"

This outcome has inevitably prompted questions about whether the Madring spectacle would have been more entertaining had the tyre compounds been a bit more on the aggressive side.

It is a nice theory that if you took away the comfort of the thermal and mechanical robustness of the C2 hard tyre the Spanish GP would have been better.

That suggests that, forced onto softer compounds, drivers would have had a more challenging time in having rubber that did not last the whole distance, thereby producing more excitement.

The idea is good, but sadly reality bites when it comes to understanding the complex factors that dictate whether races become strategic masterclasses.

First, there is a notable difference in behaviour and characteristics between the C2 and the C3, which means that, while the hard was good for the whole race, the medium was significantly not as good and much more prone to the risk of graining.

As McLaren's Oscar Piastri said: "The medium tyre was just awful. It was good for literally one lap, but then it was terrible."

Increased degradation does not automatically mean more stops though. It can (especially when overtaking is difficult) lead to more tyre management and cars running well off the pace, and you end up with the same spectacle as we got on Sunday.

Plus, one important element at Madring that will forever speak against multi-stop races is the length of the pitlane.

Swapping tyres there costs around 25 seconds - one of the biggest losses of the season - so teams are always going to try to minimise the need to change tyres.

Based on the evidence from the Madring, Pirelli felt that going a step softer with the compounds - bringing the C3/C4/C5 rather than the C2/C3/C4 - was not a way to improve the spectacle.

That is because, as Pirelli's head of motorsport, Dario Marrafuschi, pointed out, based on the struggles that drivers had with the C3 and C4 in the short stints in which they managed to keep them alive in the race, it would have simply turned the race into a major management drama.

Throw into the mix too that the Madring, thanks to the banked La Monumental and high numbers of corners, is one of the most challenging tracks on the calendar for tyres, then it would also increase the possibility of safety dangers thanks to the high levels of wear.

"It would have been a two-stop race with a high wear," Marrafuschi told The Race. "On paper you can say, 'OK, it must be a two-stopper'.

"But, because of traffic, drivers would just end up doing what Gasly did.

"It was a good choice to have the C2 as a race compound and give teams the possibility to have one-stop in case of an early safety car. The C3/C4/C5 would have been too much."

Going softer would also have caused trouble in qualifying. As it was, the C4 teams took into the fight for grid positions was screaming from overheating doing a single push lap.

The C5 would probably have fallen off a cliff and been pretty useless.

Marrafuschi added: "Even during one lap with the soft, after La Monumental, the overheating of the rear was there. If the soft was a C5, maybe you would run the risk of thermal degradation during qualifying as well. It wouldn't pay the bill."

The reality is that the margins between a race delivering a perfect strategy mix of different approaches, a nailed on easy one-stopper, and complete chaos are sometimes not very much.

With Madrid's track being super-smooth, and offering high grip, teams knew going into the race that if they could avoid the risk of graining, then the one-stop strategy was on.

If not, as one engineer said, then it would instead have turned into a chaotic, heavy-degradation, two-stop-plus graining fest.

While the latter may sound exciting, it actually risks producing something that is equally as bad: one of those grands prix where there is just an endless cycle of stops so the race has no narrative.

Some of the nailed-on elements of Madring - the smooth, high-grip surface, the forces through La Monumental, and the long pitlane - mean that unless overtaking opportunities are improved there is little that can be done to encourage more stops.

All eyes are on what track changes are done next year because opening the door for passes will be the best way to improve the strategy element too.

items.title: Audi's shrewd choice of F2 team for its first F1 junior
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Audi's first Formula 1 junior driver Freddie Slater will join forces with defending champion team Invicta in Formula 2 in 2027.

Slater narrowly missed out on the Formula 3 title at the Madring last weekend but has had a highly impressive rookie season, living up to the promise built up by strong karting success and back-to-back titles in Italian Formula 4 and the Formula Regional European Championship.

It was that early-career success that meant he had offers from multiple F1 teams to join their junior programmes from an early age.

But much like Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, Slater and his management team held off on accepting those offers too early.

At the start of this year, he accepted Audi's proposal for him to become the first driver to join its F1 driver development programme as it entered F1 in 2026.

Slater fell 14 points short of winning the F3 title, having suffered a costly mechanical failure in the Monza feature race and a nightmare Madrid title-decider that allowed chief rival Ugo Ugochukwu to take the crown instead.

Slater will now move up to F2 with Invicta, the team that has taken back-to-back championship doubles in the last two years, with Audi F1 driver Gabriel Bortoleto and McLaren reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli taking the last two drivers’ titles with it. Bortoleto and Fornaroli both also went from Trident's F3 team to Invicta's F2 team, just as Slater will.

Invicta is currently hoping to make it three out of three F2 titles this year with Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, who is seven points adrift of championship leader Nikola Tsolov. Invicta itself is also just six points off Campos in the teams' title race.

F2 has added an extra feature race to its next round in Baku amid uncertainty over its current final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Slater is set to make his debut in the post-season Abu Dhabi test, although this will likely have to be rescheduled if F1 cancels its Qatar and Abu Dhabi weekends as expected. F2 could decide to join F1 if it holds its season finale at Imola in December, as is the current back-up plan. Logically the post-season F2 test would also be held there.

"The move to Formula 2 is the natural next step for Freddie, and an important new phase of his development as a driver," Audi's driver development director Allan McNish said.

"He enjoyed a strong Formula 3 season, fighting for the title until the final round - showing his speed, racecraft and progress throughout the year.

"We are very proud of what Freddie has achieved this season and how he has developed along the way. Invicta Racing has had an excellent record in recent years, and we are delighted to be working with them.

"We believe it is the ideal environment for him, and we look forward to supporting him as he takes on this new challenge in 2027."

Invicta has been the clear benchmark team during the three years of F2's current car, but the series is introducing a heavily revised version of the car from 2027.

Slater was present at the launch of the new car at Monza, telling The Race: "I think it's mega. I think it's very exciting.

"Obviously F1 has changed a lot this year so F2 kind of needs to follow suit to progress to that ladder.

"So I'm very excited to get a go behind the wheel of one and it's going to be very interesting to see what it performs like."

Slater is the first confirmed 2027 F2 driver, but he’s expected to be joined by a number of his F3 rivals, including champion Ugochukwu.

A second-place championship finish in F3 and titles in F4 and FREC mean Slater, who is yet to drive an F1 car, has more than enough points to clear the 40-point threshold for an F1 superlicence.

items.title: Just bad luck? What really robbed Norris of Spanish GP win
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
There is little doubt, even from eventual winner Kimi Antonelli, that without the "insanely unlucky" timing of the virtual safety car, Lando Norris would have won the Spanish Grand Prix.

The reigning Formula 1 world champion had built up a comfortable advantage at the head of the Madring field when Lance Stroll’s Aston Martin stopped in the run off at Turn 20 as the leaders were on lap 14 of 57.

Norris was around five seconds past the pitlane entry, and well around the final corner, when race control called for a VSC to allow Stroll’s car to be recovered.

At that point it was too late for Norris to get into the pits for a change of tyres and capitalise on the reduced time loss of doing so while the field was slowed by the VSC. Meanwhile 6.5-seconds further back, Antonelli was perfectly positioned to dive in.

With the VSC remaining out as Norris toured around slowly, committed to going for his stop at the end of the following lap.

But just before he entered Turn 21, the final right hander before the pit entry, the VSC ended. It meant that, in taking his stop, Norris lost the maximum stop time of around 25 seconds – hampered further by a slow tyre change.

That dropped him to fifth behind George Russell. Despite the clear pace advantage he showed early on, Norris’s fate was sealed by two factors: tyre degradation on the hard was negligible and overtaking was nearly impossible unless there was a big tyre offset.

Had passing been on, then McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was in no doubt about what the race outcome would have been.

"I think if overtaking was possible today, we would have had Lando again in the lead because the pace advantage was significant," he said.

In the end, Norris came home third, behind Antonelli (who acknowledged he was lucky) and Max Verstappen.

While the timing of the VSC could not have been crueller in hurting Norris to the max – coming out too late for him to respond and finishing too early for him to benefit – McLaren will still analyse if it could have handled the situation better.

And there are two key questions that it will seek answers to over the coming days.

Should it have pre-empted the VSC?

With the benefit of hindsight, it is obvious to say that the best way for McLaren to have saved Norris’s Spanish GP win would have been to stop the moment the Stroll situation was developing.

While it is true that there was nothing McLaren could have done to react quicker to the VSC being triggered, as Norris was well past the pit entry when it was called, an element it does want to understand better is if there was a way to predict where things were heading.

So when it sits down at Woking to dig through the details, it will want to understand if there was enough information from the state and location of Stroll’s car to pre-empt that the situation was going to switch from a double yellow to VSC imminently.

Stroll’s car, having suffered a brake problem, had come to a halt pointing towards a gap in the barriers – but had not gone all the way through it.

Norris had been warned over the radio shortly before arriving about there being a yellow flag, but there did not seem to be any indication that this would be a serious incident.

Once Stroll had jumped out the car, race control was happy that the marshals were ready to retrieve the Aston Martin and push it through the gap.

It is when track officials are exposed on the other side of the barriers that triggers a double yellow incident being escalated to VSC.

So was this step from a double yellow to a VSC something that McLaren could have predicted?

Based on the positioning of Stroll’s car, probably not. 

There was no major damage, no debris scattered everywhere and the AMR26 was only a few metres from safety.

So it is debatable if there was enough information in the less than 20 seconds McLaren had between being aware Stroll had stopped and the chance to make a pitstop call to be convinced that this was going to trigger a caution period.

Had it opted to go for a stop, and then race control managed to deal with Stroll’s car under double yellows, McLaren would have been lambasted for throwing a win away.

As Stella later explained: "If you get it wrong, it would be extremely penalising. From the lead, you pit unnecessarily and now you lost the victory.

"I think a good rule is to respond to what is a fact, to what is the real condition of the circuit.

"But we will definitely take a look as to whether in these conditions it was just simply obvious that it would end up in a virtual safety car. I cannot answer at the moment."

But what was not known to McLaren at the time as well was that race control’s decisions about going for the VSC option was influenced by a desire to clear up debris on the track at Turn 5 as well.

Parts of carbon fibre left on the circuit at the chicane, most likely from the collision between Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz on lap 12, posed a clear risk of causing punctures and there was a desire to remove it – which would require a VSC.

So with Stroll’s car in the position it was, the decision to go for the caution was based on the double influence of the Aston Martin and the track debris at the other side of the circuit.

This also explains why there was nearly one minute between Stroll's car being behind the barriers and the VSC ending.

While pre-empting the VSC would obviously have been the right thing to do, there would have been no way for McLaren to know about all the influences race control had in its decisions – especially the Turn 5 debris.

Should McLaren have kept Norris out?

With the VSC out and Norris past the pitlane entry, there was nothing McLaren could do before he came around again.

It made a call to bring him in that lap, obviously in the hope that the VSC continued so the deficit to those who had stopped on the previous lap was equalised.

McLaren thought until the last second that the extended VSC was due to marshals being on the track, but as Norris rolled into Turn 21 the caution period ended.

Norris was 10 seconds from the pitlane entry at this point but the team committed to seeing through on its decision to stop – even though it meant it would lose the full 25s plus what it took for a tyre change.

The subsequent slow stop, which cost more time, ultimately changed little as McLaren thinks Norris would still have returned to the track behind Russell.

The obvious question to be asked here is whether McLaren should have abandoned the stop and pushed on to build up more of a gap – and then changed tyres a few laps later.

The theory is nice based on the pace early on, but the reality was that the tyre situation in the race meant it was never going to prove beneficial.

The hard that many of the cars behind had switched to had proved to be a very robust tyre, with minimal degradation and not needing too much management.

The medium, which Norris was on at this stage, was much more fragile – so after 15 laps of running would not have been in condition for him to get his head down and build up a buffer.

So while things had looked comfortable in terms of the gap to Antonelli prior to the stops, both were coming to the end of their usable tyre life.

As one rival team said about managing the different tyres: "You could drive the medium slowly, or you could go fast and they would be gone after 10 laps."

There is also a small element that, even with the VSC ending, stopping then still has advantages over one in normal racing conditions.

Norris said: "It's the fact that everyone’s kind of on colder tyres and you’re still minimising the pit loss. But the medium tyre was destroyed and the hard tyre was amazing."

As Stella explained after the race, if Norris had stayed out, the upside was minimal.

"We considered staying out," he said. "But you have to accept the fact that now you are on relatively used medium tyres and the people behind you will be on new hards. So you're never going to open a gap on people on a new hard.

"Therefore, we kind of needed to accept that that was what we should have done. It was incredibly unfortunate."

There was little else that McLaren could have done to change the outcome – as Stella ultimately concluded that his squad suffered from a paradox of being too fast.

Had its race pace not been so good, and Norris not had those six seconds over Antonelli, then he would have been in the perfect spot to dive into the pits when the VSC was called to win the race.

But F1 is not about going slower – and McLaren ultimately knows that it was just a case of wrong place, wrong time.

As Stella reflected on Sunday night: "We take it on the chin that what we could not control just played against us."

items.title: Edd Straw's 2026 Spanish Grand Prix F1 driver rankings
items.author: Edd Straw
items.content:
The inaugural Formula 1 race at the Madring was no classic - but the Spanish Grand Prix weekend as a whole did seriously test the grid.

Here's who passed with flying colours, and who was found wanting...

- Put in a mighty qualifying lap to take an unexpected pole position in what McLaren is certain wasn't the fastest car.

- Held onto the lead at the start despite the lower grip level in the pole position grid box compared to second place, and built a healthy lead in the early stages.

- Would have won without the virtual safety car being perfectly-timed to cost him the lead as he was the fastest in race conditions.

- The rear stepping out at the last corner cost him three tenths in Q3, and denied him a potential all-time great qualifying lap. That was down to him misjudging how much his mighty lap up to then impacted tyre condition, but shows he didn't deliver the maximum possible.

- Couldn't get past Verstappen in the closing stages. But considering how difficult overtaking was for everyone and how difficult Verstappen is to pass generally, that's not something he could have done much about.

Only bad luck cost him victory.

- Recovered from an alarming moment in La Monumental on his first Q2 run to put in a superb lap on his last run, "one of the best I've done", to top the midfield and reach Q3, outpacing team-mate Pierre Gasly.

- Achieved the best-possible qualifying position for an Alpine by defeating Arvid Lindblad in Q3.

- Drove a strong race to head the midfield pack, and overachieved by one place by holding off Oscar Piastri.

- Left a fraction on the table in Q3 and was the driver with the biggest deficit to his theoretical best lap at 0.204s. Not that it made any difference to his position.

- Had he been able to pass Gabriel Bortoleto, then Liam Lawson was beatable but given the overtaking challenge that's not a big negative.

Probably his best through-weekend execution in F1.

13th 11th

- Put in a good qualifying effort on his final Q2 lap, with the three-tenths gap to Bortoleto suggesting that in qualifying conditions the Haas wasn't quite at the level of the Audi.

- Made a characteristically good start and jumped to 11th ahead of the Audis, which put him 10th once Lewis Hamilton retired early.

- But for losing a place to Nico Hulkenberg in the VSC pitstops due to Haas's pit equipment not being as advanced as Audi's, he would almost certainly have scored a point.

- Ollie Bearman's self-inflicted absence from qualifying and poor grid position make comparisons difficult, but there's nothing to suggest Ocon was leaving any significant laptime on the table.

A well-executed weekend that merited a points finish in probably the eighth-best car.

- While the Red Bull was stronger in qualifying conditions than on race pace, he got close to the maximum out of the car on Saturday - even if, as for most, there was maybe a little left on the table.

- Even on a track where passing is difficult, did a good job to keep Norris behind.

- While luck assisted him in the path to second, even if he'd stayed in third without jumping Norris it would have probably been about as much as was possible.

- Given the first-corner move was always likely to lead to a chicane cut, you can argue that this led to him being behind Antonelli, who was the other beneficiary of Verstappen having to let Hamilton past.

Largely made the most of the Red Bull.

- Was clearly the faster Mercedes driver, with his pace advantage over George Russell clear-cut.

- The vast majority of his race was well-executed, showing patience when holding position while long-running Leclerc led.

- Needed luck on his side to win, as this gave him track position over Verstappen and Norris.

- The frenetic first lap featured track cuts at Turn 1 and Turn 5, which led to him being shuffled back to third.

No question about his pace, but a little untidiness.

- Despite the self-inflicted disadvantage of having to run some old-spec power unit components as a result of his Monza crash, he was just 0.005s down on Hamilton in qualifying.

- Drove a good, clean race and did what he could in his lengthy hard stint, although ultimately the car pace meant that he was always likely to finish fourth once Hamilton had retired.

- Probably left a little pace on the table in qualifying, particularly early in the lap owing to the prep laps not being perfectly executed, but as he put it, still delivered "quite a clean lap" albeit with "a few moments here and there".

No major negatives, but still didn't look at his absolute best.

- While the huge advantage over Valtteri Bottas was inflated by his team-mate being impeded by Carlos Sainz on his final lap, Perez always looked destined to be the faster Cadillac in qualifying. And he executed well, with a strong final lap.

- Drove a strong race before a water leak in the power unit led to him first slowing then retiring, having gained places to the Turn 1 incident then chased Alex Albon.

- The only real downside is that he didn't have the chance to run the second half of the race, which wasn't his fault.

A strong weekend when he was the quicker Cadillac driver.

16th 15th

- Recovered superbly from practice troubles and his FP3 mistake to put in a strong Q1 lap. Although the advantage over Sainz was infinitesimal at 0.005s, that was a big step forward.

- Williams didn't have the pace to have done any better than 16th in qualifying, especially given Albon didn't have a fresh set of softs left for Q2.

- Drove a good race in a car that didn't have the pace to do any better.

- Struggled on Friday with deployment problems that put him on the back foot and well off Sainz's pace.

- Clipping the wall early in FP3 cost him important running.

A strong weekend, with the FP3 wall-clip the one negative.

17th 17th

- Always looked like the faster Aston Martin driver throughout the weekend.

- Was able to show the strength of the car in certain corners, which was offset by time lost on the straights.

- Battled on to the finish despite deployment troubles and a front wing change after being hit by Sainz.

- He was a tenth and a half off his personal best in sector three on his final lap, which was sufficient to swing the battle for Q2 with Albon against him.

- Race problems meant he was compromised, losing significant race time.

A decent weekend, but perhaps could have got the Aston Martin into Q2.

- While qualifying wasn't maximised, it still represented a decent recovery after his FP3 off cost him his simulation.

- Probably had the stronger underlying pace of the Ferrari drivers, although didn't make the most of it.

- Crash in FP3 cost him half of that session and his qualifying simulation run, despite his best efforts to get back to the pits against the team's instructions.

- Didn't make the most of qualifying with a small error early in the lap that cost him time.

Had the pace to achieve more, but compromised Saturday then brake misfortune meant he didn't show it.

- Showed strong pace on Friday before his crash, but despite admitting to still being down on confidence in qualifying he made Q3.

- Ran ahead of Piastri in the first stint after jumping him on the opening lap.

- Managed to hold off Hulkenberg late on.

- FP2 crash at Turn 13 when the rear end gave up immediately on turn-in cost him some running on a day when he was quick, with a hangover that led to him not joining FP3 until the closing stages.

- Couldn't hold Piastri off after the McLaren driver had made his pitstop, but considering the advantage of fresh mediums there's no disgrace in that.

FP2 crash had significant consequences, but Lindblad recovered well.

11th 10th

- Won the battle of imperfect execution with his team-mate in Q2 by 0.165s.

- Made the most of starting on softs and the timing of the VSC to take a point.

- Was the slightly better Audi driver when everything is taken into account.

- There might have been a way to get past Lindblad late on, but hardly a big negative considering the difficulty of passing.

- Didn't make the most of the car in qualifying, as slipping into Q3 was possible.

A solid weekend's work, putting the Audi broadly where it should have been.

- Made an important pass on Colapinto early on, albeit having lost the place at the start.

- Stayed out on hards under the VSC, and made that strategy work decently to capitalise on Bortoleto holding up Colapinto to finish ahead of him.

- Again struggled to follow Verstappen's pace steps as qualifying progressed, ending up a respectable but disappointed 0.352s down.

- With the caveat that it's only his third outing in the Red Bull, he was very much in the group of top-team second drivers as defined by pace.

Solid but unspectacular, with an unobtrusively effective race drive.

- Was one of the few drivers to make a successful overtaking move by passing Lawson after he made his second pitstop.

- Had a clean weekend and was on the wrong side of the VSC in terms of having started on the hard tyres - although that was a deliberate choice to open up the possibility of staying out if there was an early interruption. This was closed off when Leclerc ahead did the same thing, leading to Russell stopping and then, thanks to the mediums not having the range, having to make a second pitstop.

- There was no hint of him being at Antonelli's level throughout the weekend.

- Asked a little too much of the tyres at Turn 11 on his final Q3 lap, which cost him time but he was already gradually slipping back from Antonelli prior to that.

A step back from Antonelli in terms of pace.

- Wasn't at fault for the front-wing damage on the opening lap that compromised his race.

- Managed to pass Lindblad after making his pitstop, having run the hard/medium strategy without a VSC stop.

- Simply wasn't at Norris's level in terms of pace.

- Couldn't find a way past Colapinto in the closing stages.

A lacklustre weekend.

12th 13th

- Drove a tidy long stint on hards, keeping the quicker Colapinto behind him.

- Was unlucky with the VSC timing given he had started on hards.

- Wasn't at his best in qualifying, admitting he didn't extract the maximum from the car with being a little too conservative into Turn 1 putting him on the back foot versus Hulkenberg.

- Poor start dropped him down to 15th, but that's mitigated by the fact he was on hard Pirellis.

A middling weekend, marginally worse than Hulkenberg's.

14th 12th

- Showed good pace in the race, but the timing of the VSC meant he stayed out on hards and that didn't allow him to translate it into points.

- His underlying speed was, save for when it really mattered in qualifying, where you'd expect it to be.

- Lacklustre in qualifying, expressing bafflement at a car that felt good in FP3 struggling for grip in qualifying thanks to poor tyre prep on the outlap.

- Picked up a five-second penalty added at the end of the race for speeding in the pits, which was needless although it only cost him time, not a position.

Poor qualifying defined his weekend.

19th 18th

- The 2.098s qualifying deficit to Perez was completely unrepresentative because Bottas had to rely on his first-run time, with the second ruined by traffic and the third by Sainz impeding him.

- Looked the slower Cadillac driver overall.

- Race gave him little opportunity to shine given the damage he picked up through no fault of his own.

Had bad luck in both qualifying and the race, but didn't look to be at Perez's level.

- Ran ahead of Alonso for a couple of laps early on before falling behind him approaching Turn 13.

- Brake troubles and damage from debris meant that the race comparison with Alonso doesn't mean anything.

- Had no opportunity in qualifying given a water leak prevented him setting a time in Q1, but there was nothing before that to suggest he would have been close to Alonso's pace.

- Single-lap pace ultimately wasn't a factor for Stroll given he had a 40-place grid penalty for power-unit element changes, which limited his opportunities to impress. That context significantly mitigates the negative of the fact he didn't show anything like Alonso's single-lap pace through practice.

No chance in qualifying or the race, but also no glimmers of Alonso-like pace elsewhere.

15th 14th

- Considering the damage, his race pace was respectable, but losing time behind Perez early on limited his horizons.

- Struggled in qualifying, with the 0.880s deficit to Lindblad down to Tsunoda being far happier with the car on scrubbed tyres than fresh ones. This meant he couldn't exploit the peak of the available grip and was therefore nowhere.

- Damage at the first corner from being clobbered by Sainz meant there was no opportunity to recover from a difficult qualifying.

A nothing weekend thanks to qualifying struggles and race damage.

- Showed good pace on Friday and seemed on form heading into qualifying.

- While the pitwall takes the responsibility for being oblivious to Bottas's presence and not warning Sainz, the driver always has to take a small share of the blame, even with visibility limited.

- Qualified behind Albon (by 0.005s) but pointed to poor timing of the final run and a straightline deficit as holding him back.

- Was caught out by the inevitable Turn 1 concertina at the start then compromised his race by hitting Alonso.

Pace was fine, but too many errors.

22nd (pits) 16th

- Drove a good race from the pitlane, although his two on-track passes were of the damaged Bottas and Stroll.

- Crashing heavily in FP3 after tagging the inside wall in the Turn 10/11 sweep caused a major accident - and came after a warning on Friday when he clipped the front-left at Turn 15 with less serious consequences. It also cost him qualifying.

As he said, "I have only myself to blame" for the shunt that defined his weekend.

items.title: San Marino Grand Prix MotoGP rider rankings 2026
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
The San Marino Grand Prix weekend at Misano was dominated by Spaniards - and so are our MotoGP rider rankings for the weekend. But which of the two clear standouts leads the way this time?

2nd 1st 1st

For the second weekend running the 2027 Ducati line-up monopolises the top two in these rankings - and this time Marquez gets the nod, again by the narrowest of margins.

He had claimed on Friday he would "sign right now" for a podium and that Marco Bezzecchi was the favourite - and whether that was 'mind games-y' or not, the claim did seem backed up by what was going on on track.

But a bet on the medium rear combined with another great approach to Turn 1 at the start won Marquez the sprint - and he controlled the main race after Bezzecchi's exit.

At a track which doles out a real punishment to the right side of the body - where Marquez is compromised - he was the top Ducati in every session.

7th 6th 3rd

The standards remain sky high for Acosta, who got his customary Friday crash out of the way early on and subsequently was again on another level compared to his fellow KTM riders.

He lamented losing ground in a Fermin Aldeguer battle in the sprint - in which he claimed both were doing "stupid s**t" - and was generally unhappy with the stopping performance of his RC16.

But a "disaster"-esque warm-up on Sunday was followed up by a fantastic ride in the grand prix, delivering another podium that had never felt on the cards for KTM.

3rd8th 4th

Aldeguer had a technical issue on Friday that cost him a real shot at Q2, so did it the hard way on Saturday morning - powering to third on the grid in one of his best qualifying efforts yet in MotoGP.

He got roughed up a bit on the sprint, by Acosta but particularly by Raul Fernandez, and then coped much better in the main race with the field more spread out and the pace clearly strong.

Given Misano is so demanding physically, and Aldeguer is still injury-limited (and also riding an old bike), this was a triumph of a weekend.

6th 9th 9th

Marini's best weekend of the year, the high point of it a Q2 run to a spectacular sixth on the grid - which he did admit was probably aided by yellow-flag timings and others messing up.

Never one for excessive modesty, he described himself as "every time faster than my team-mates" this weekend - and the two races bore that out.

He was "giving everything" on Sunday to keep Fabio Di Giannantonio at bay - laughing that "for sure he hates me!" given the defensive lines, though Di Giannantonio saw no issue with it and was full of praise for his friend. Ultimately, that defensive effort was for naught, a late-race vibration in the rear forcing Marini to simply drag the bike to the finish.

9th 5th 2nd

Super-fast again, the younger Marquez had performance for a front-row start and should have been in the mix to snipe a win.

A two-crash Q2, in which he was wrong-footed by adjusting to a new soft tyre after running used rubber in preceding practice, was a hammer blow to his hopes of a truly amazing result.

Still, he recovered well in both races, so well that many went away after Sunday's contest wondering whether he really should have worked his way past his brother and put himself in position to win.

5th3rd 5th

This was so nearly an almighty smash-and-grab by Martin, who went from trailing Aprilia team-mate Bezzecchi by six tenths of a second in qualifying to being in position to win the race and extend his championship lead.

Whether he would've won the race without his compartment syndrome issue is conjecture at this point - but he certainly he feels he could have, and he feels that his title charge is emboldened by this weekend, as long as he can suitably address this arm issue, through surgery or management.

There is still a very substantial single-lap question mark - 0.546s off on Friday, 0.587s off on Saturday is a losing formula - but there's something to be said for how deftly he was navigating the race circumstances this weekend.

4th 4th 7th

Di Giannantonio was pacing for a front row (or maybe even better) after three corners of his final Q2 lap, then went down in Turn 4.

But it didn't compromise his grid position too much, and that anyway didn't seem all that important to the outcome of his weekend.

Much more impactful was that early grand prix melee that dropped him into the mid-pack - with Aldeguer squeezing him to the outside kerb at Turn 1 in the inciting incident - and a subsequent brake-lever concern that limited his ability to overtake back up the order.

13th 21st 10th

Make no mistake - after the unseemly business of his stroppy back-and-forth with Yamaha at Aragon, Quartararo properly showed up at Misano.

That was easy to overlook given his most notable moment of the weekend was a clumsy fall on the sprint while trying to set up a move on Diogo Moreira - but this indirectly will have been a consequence of being the only Yamaha rider with the potential to do anything of note. Of the 11 1m31s laps delivered by Yamahas in the sprint, Quartararo was responsible for all 11.

"It's clear he has more than us this weekend," admitted team-mate Alex Rins, usually not one to acknowledge it so plainly.

Quartararo's grand prix was more muted in terms of performance, due to a need to conserve fuel - but given that he stood his ground impressively in the top 10.

10th 7th 6th

Fernandez wasn't perfect, but clearly wasn't given the best opportunities to make much of this weekend. A return of seventh and sixth in the two races is kind of the bare minimum given the level of the Aprilia, but he can't really be faulted.

He did labour a bit on Friday, with errors in crucial moments, but navigated Q1 well - including a massive "one in 15" save tucking the front at Turn 1. But in Q2 there was a "problem on both bikes", so he was well off his Q1 time and grid position-limited, conditioning both races.

An unexpected fuel-consumption problem on Sunday meant he was in the lean engine map for virtually the whole thing and never got the chance to pick off the arm-pump-limited Martin or show much of anything.

16th15th 8th

Bastianini just missed out on Friday on what would have been a weekend-transforming top-10 place. He had decided against fitting a fresh front tyre for his final time attack - which is not an unconventional decision, but in his case it proved "a big mistake".

The pace was probably there to do better (he set his fastest lap of the grand prix, and a very good one at that, on the final lap, in typical Bastianini fashion) but from 16th on the grid it was never really on the cards, and even for all these caveats there is little doubt the transcendent Acosta had much more performance.

12th 16th 14th

'The world's fastest journalist', or whatever they say, lived up to the billing this weekend by grabbing onto the back of Acosta and powering to a great Q2 appearance.

But that 'journalist' quip is increasingly more relevant. It has been a long, long while since Espargaro has raced regularly and it is showing. He "missed the aggression to overtake" on Saturday, and Sunday's race exhausted him.

He was all too keenly aware at the end that he was a 35-year-old fighting against a grid of largely 20-somethings. "My respect to Marc Marquez and Johann Zarco!" he laughed.

21st 18th 12th

The best laptime of Razgatlioglu's weekend came in the grand prix, on lap 12. If you know your MotoGP, you know this is extremely suboptimal in terms of extracting a positive result.

He said knowledge of Misano from World Superbike "did not help" here, and his one-lap pace was extremely poor, particularly in a "very bad" Q1.

But the race pace was obviously there, at a fairly high level. He was the top Yamaha on the road, in the sprint, though lost a position for track limits, then was right with Yamaha benchmark Quartararo in the grand prix - though again fell foul of track limits, even if the resulting long lap didn't actually cost him a position.

11th 10th DNF

The follow-up at Misano was more like what we all would have expected from Zarco's comeback weekend at Aragon - and even so, the actual speed was fairly decent.

Zarco navigated Friday well to land in Q2, but this was probably flattering his ultimate potential race trim. Still, he could have been much higher on the grid had he improved on his second Q2 run - and had he avoided a penalty for impeding Bezzecchi, which he acknowledged as "totally fair".

He got stuck behind a fuel-managing Quartararo on Sunday before missing his braking at Turn 8 late on and going down.

17th 20th DNF

Mir was markedly slower than usual relative to his fellow Honda riders, but this seemed to have less to do with a lack of confidence on braking he reported on Friday and more to do with some sort of unspecified ailment that increasingly bothered him over the weekend.

Suffering from a headache and with no strength, he gutted it through a fruitless sprint but had to give up very early in the main race, fearing that riding around "would only make the situation worse".

He now has medical tests to do between here and the Red Bull Ring to properly figure out his situation.

15th11th DNF

After a run of really strong form of late, Misano was largely a letdown for Moreira.

For most of the weekend, the third sector - and Curvone in particular - was the culprit, as he and LCR struggled to stabilise the Honda sufficiently in the fast right-hander.

He said after the sprint: "I told Honda, tomorrow we're cutting this corner, I don't care!" But Moreira actually made a bit of a breakthrough there in Sunday warm-up, then fell off right away on Sunday without managing to properly confirm his work.

1st 2nd DNF

This one will sting for a while.

A 37-point weekend looked on the cards for Bezzecchi after his blistering record lap in Q2 - but it turned into a nine-pointer instead, with defeat in the sprint and catastrophe in the main race.

He seemed in a real hurry to break away from Marquez and the rest of them at the start of the grand prix, but with the bike unsettled through Curvone and the subsequent Turn 12 he arrived at Turn 13 compromised and lost the front.

Forget about this being a home race or whatever. This is a monumental blow for his championship.

19th14th 11th

"Not fast enough" was Binder's summary through the weekend and at the end of it. His qualifying was "a bit s**t" and his race pace was generally underwhelming, but he did spare his KTM team any repair bills and finished in the points.

He's pacing for an inglorious, ill-fitting conclusion to his MotoGP tenure - but is at least just quietly struggling rather than properly imploding. Or is it better to burn out than to fade away (my my, hey hey)?

8th 12th 13th

Despite lacking confidence again with the Ducati GP25, Morbidelli looked notably more competitive than for most of his difficult final season in MotoGP. He gets a bit of credit for this - but it gets almost entirely offset by the fact he didn't capitalise on the opportunity.

Another instance of impeding a fellow rider - this time Bastianini on Friday - needlessly capped his Sunday potential by virtue of a long lap penalty, meaning Saturday was the best shot at a headline result.

But no such luck. He looked uncharacteristically timid in the early laps of the sprint, roughed up a bit by Moreira and then forced to spend the rest of the race shadowing the LCR Honda rider without a way past.

20th 19th DNF

Friday had looked gently encouraging but proved a mirage as Rins ultimately just didn't have all that much performance to offer this weekend - and was not happy with the bike.

He was only ever in play for some attrition-aided points on Sunday but became part of said attrition, parking up as he suffered from a "migraine and severe nausea".

18th17th DNF

A freak "cold brakes, cold tyres" crash at Rio literally something like 30 seconds into the weekend set the tone for Miller.

He just wasn't very competitive, chasing the right set-up all throughout and falling off in the grand prix as early as lap two shortly after a ding-dong battle with Zarco.

He said the bike felt improved on Sunday but "I didn't get to do bugger all on it".

14th13thDNF

Favourable track, unfavourable track, home track, foreign track, left-handers, right-handers, hard braking, high-speed - suddenly it just doesn't seem to matter at all.

This is the third time in a row (and yet only the third time this season) that Bagnaia sits lower than 20th in these rankings. He has looked all wrong since his arm-pump surgery - though he clearly seems of the opinion this is more coincidence than causation.

"It's extremely easy to see the difference between what my bike is doing compared to all the other Ducatis. Big, big difference, but difficult to understand why," Bagnaia lamented in-weekend, hitting a familiar note. He could not extract rear grip and struggled to stay on the bike, feeling "humiliated" by the experience.

The Turn 2 crash in the grand prix delivered a coup de grace to this terrible weekend - but who's to say it will be any better in Austria?

items.title: Everything we learned from F1's 2026 Spanish Grand Prix
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
But that's not to say the weekend was a dud: the track proved a hit with drivers, and away from it there were significant revelations - about this year's title fight, but also involving the bid to keep one of F1's star drivers in the championship.

Here are our main takeaways from the Madring:

Hamilton's title bid is over

You may not have felt like there was a realistic Lewis Hamilton/Ferrari 2026 F1 title bid ongoing for a while (or, if you're sceptical, ever) but there was a notable change in tone from Hamilton about it after his early retirement with brake problems in Madrid.

In recent weeks his warnings to Ferrari over its management of races and its drivers had been all about how the title shot was getting more distant at best.

But when Sky Sports F1 put it to him in Madrid that Kimi Antonelli "looks hard to stop now", Hamilton pretty much congratulated his Mercedes replacement on the 2026 title.

"There's no stopping him and Mercedes this year," said Hamilton. "I think they've done a phenomenal job and they deserve it."

Which was about two steps further down that road than he really needed to go in the circumstances. The fact Hamilton went there shows that - at least in the immediate disgruntlement of his early Madrid retirement - the last title hope is now gone in his mind.

With the deficit now up to 101 points and few signs lately of Ferrari having Mercedes-beating pace, it would be hard to imagine any other scenario.

Aston Martin really needs some Honda help

It emerged at the Madring that FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has been speaking to Fernando Alonso and Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll about the prospect of giving Honda some extra help to boost its recovery plan.

The Madring weekend exposed yet again that Honda is lacking - even though it is a far less power-sensitive circuit than Monza.

Alonso said "the engine was very bad today" after the race, saying he almost stalled at the pitstops because of an engine issue. He also reported the power unit was struggling to recover when he was slowing to respect blue flags.

So a boost for Honda can't come soon enough, and we know there isn't another major Honda upgrade coming until 2027.

Any such extra help - be it homologation freedoms, extra spending allowances, or specific rule changes in areas where Honda is failing to make progress - will require the support of other power unit manufacturers.

The good thing for Aston Martin Honda is that both Mercedes and Red Bull were receptive to the idea of once again assisting Honda, as its rivals did earlier this year.

Exactly how, what they may leverage in return, and where everyone stands in private, remains to be seen.

But the Madring was a stark reminder of how welcome that help would be right now.

Red Bull's car is still degrading

The mysterious 'car degradation' problems afflicting Red Bull this season aren't going away, based on both Max Verstappen and team principal Laurent Mekies' comments in Madrid.

Red Bull is still not offering any insight on precisely what the problem is, but Mekies admitted it's still there, has been for a long time, and will be for the rest of the season.

"There is an element of car performance degradation that is happening through a session and through a race," said Mekies.

"He's [Verstappen is] right in saying it's not a new issue. We are not sleeping on it. We have been trying to tackle that in different ways.

"Obviously, I consider it a complex issue, otherwise we would get to the bottom of it. But everyone is very constructive about it and tries to make small steps at the time to be able to get to the bottom of it eventually.

"We had a couple of positive steps in that regard this weekend. It will never be the full picture, but we certainly have - through pain - made progress in our understanding.

"We don't have all the solutions yet in the car, but I trust that we are on the right way. It will not be fast, so it's something that will probably take us through next year."

This wasn't the ideal Madring layout

As you may have seen, The Race revealed on Monday that three key areas of the track have been identified for improvement to increase the prospect of overtaking after a race bereft of passing.

What we've also learned is that those revisions - to the Turn 5 braking zone at the end of the first sector, the Turn 13 left-hander after La Monumental, and the tight Turn 20 - had already been proposed to the FIA before this year's race.

That they weren't implemented for its F1 debut, and are being made for 2027 instead, comes down to two factors: the complexities of track simulations, and complicated homologation processes.

The construction of the Madring was already tight, time-wise - work started in April last year - and was delayed by a wet winter in Madrid.

So, the safer option was to avoid any changes so no extra delays were built into the homologation process that could've hindered the construction work and opened the door to much bigger issues had the track not been ready in time.

In the case of the Madring, that process also required the involvement of local authorities. Consider that road, rail, and aviation stakeholders all needed to be consulted, alongside emergency officials and water, drainage, and other environmental agencies, and you can see why this was a risk-averse first race on this 'street' circuit.

But expect the Madring to look a little different when F1 returns next Autumn.

This isn't the end of Williams's 2026 pain

Williams awaits its big 2026 upgrade at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix but Alex Albon doesn’t think it will be enough to turn the team into a midfield contender.

Albon had another frustrating race in Madrid where he probably maximised the package, but still finished 15th, while Carlos Sainz retired with damage.

Albon said he was "just waiting for Baku" - but changed his tone when asked by The Race's Edd Straw what he was expecting from the step.

"We're finishing, really simply, 50 seconds behind the midfield at the minute in the race - so we're losing a second a lap more or less in the race, and it needs to be a pretty big upgrade to do it [wipe out that gap]," he said.

"All we know, it's going to be a good step, but is it going to be the full step? I'm hopeful for it, but I don't think it would be.

"Unfortunately, we said it last year, but the focus is on next year as well, and we realise we're too far back at the moment to have a couple of upgrades for this year. We need to focus on next year."

He added that the rate of development among the midfield has seen some teams bring "three or four upgrades a year" recently, and said some of those upgrades are "huge".

Alpine made a big step back to the front of that pack with its Dutch GP package, and Haas made progress with its Monza upgrade - and both teams are already in front of Williams.

Albon explained: "If you think of us in a normal year, Baku would have put us back in contention, but we have to be honest with ourselves, the speed of the development race this year is huge, and we've fallen back."

It is therefore unlikely that Williams will contend for points in Azerbaijan and add to its tally of 11 - but previous editions of that race have proven chaotic.

Gasly's Monza pole catalysed Colapinto

The elation from Pierre Gasly's pole position at Monza might have been short-lived given he was quickly consumed by faster rivals in the race, but that Saturday result did prove useful for Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto.

At Madrid, Colapinto qualified ninth and finished seventh ahead of McLaren's Oscar Piastri, with another great start off the line.

He was particularly pleased with his execution of the Madrid weekend - and credited it to learnings gained from Gasly's Monza pole.

"After Monza, I learned a lot of the quali of Pierre and I tried to do a step here. And I did it. And I maximised everything again," he said, when asked by The Race's Edd Straw whether this was his best F1 weekend in terms of execution.

"The quali was one of the best I've done. With very, very, very perfect laps. And putting the car in Q3 - that was always a bit tricky with the Audis going very fast here. And today, we stayed in front in the race and scored a lot of points.

"So, very happy. Again, it's extremely positive. And I'm very happy with the pace and the results."

He explained that Gasly's experience gave him useful information "on everything" in terms of qualifying execution in Madrid.

"On driving and energy management, from run to run, from Q1 to Q2 to Q3, were very clear. And yeah, I learned from that.

"Here, I was really on it in qualifying. On a very difficult track. Probably the most difficult one of the year to nail a lap. And also the most satisfying one when you do it. And both Q2 and Q3 were amazing laps."

It's happy days at Alpine, with Gasly - who was 12th after waiting until the end of the race to pit - also buoyed for Baku.

"Honestly, the pace was insane after that VSC [virtual safety car]. I think it's really positive," he claimed.

Haas is close to ending points drought

Haas hasn't scored a point since the Monaco GP in early June, but it did come very close to ending that dry spell in Madrid.

The car inconsistency issues that have plagued Haas all season weren't present here and Esteban Ocon was running 10th in the early stages.

But he was then jumped in the pitlane under the virtual safety car by Nico Hulkenberg because of an Audi pitstop that, in terms of time spent in the pitlane, was 1.133s faster than Haas's.

"We lost out on the pitstop against Audi, but I don't believe it was our team's fault; it's really the equipment that we need to improve to give them a better chance," Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu explained.

That dropped Ocon just out of the net points-paying positions, leaving him 11th at the chequered flag despite a late push.

But Ocon still felt that was an overachievement, saying "we extracted more than what the car could do" even if he was "sad at the same time because we could have got a point".

Team-mate Ollie Bearman couldn't do the same after the FP3 crash that ensured he missed qualifying, started from the pitlane and ended up 16th.

But Bearman thinks Baku will suit the upgraded Haas as it hopes to fend off an Audi team that's been slowly chipping away at Haas's points advantage in the fight for seventh in the constructors' championship.

items.title: Three changes Madring will make after terrible F1 debut
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Spanish Grand Prix chiefs are planning changes in three key areas of the Madring circuit for 2027, The Race can reveal, off the back of its processional Formula 1 debut.

F1 drivers' worst fears were realised on Sunday when it proved ultra-difficult for cars to pass one another at the Madring, triggering a far-from-thrilling spectacle.

Not taking into account the first lap shuffling, there were hardly any overtakes at all.

While there is no official count made by F1 on the number of passes, everything points to it being the worst of the season when it comes to changes of position on track.

There are suggestions the number of passes was below even Monaco, where 10 in-race overtakes were completed.

The most notable ones were limited to Liam Lawson getting past Franco Colapinto and George Russell passing Lawson.

Although some of the stilted action was a consequence of a lack of tyre degradation on the hard compound, which meant there was not much offset strategy and performance from the rubber, the main reason for the lack of excitement was that the is no obvious overtaking spot.

For while the overall Madring layout, which included the banked La Monumental corner, was praised as being super-challenging for qualifying, the lack of passing places had been obvious in the build up to the race.

The most likely location to overtake, which was the Turn 5/6 chicane after the long run down from the opening sequence of corners, ended up being shaped in a way that deterred passing.

This was due to it having a tight entry which, as Haas driver Ollie Bearman said ahead of the weekend, meant that an overtake would never really be on.

"That kind of curved braking takes away any possibility of different lines and sending one up the inside," he said. "So that's a shame and maybe a bit of an oversight."

It is understood that this design had been settled on because of safety considerations regarding the speed and angle of approach of cars towards the tunnel section here.

Madring officials are not blind to the lack of action in the race, and The Race has learned that changes are planned in three areas for 2027 aimed at improving overtaking.

Discussions are now set to take place between the circuit and the FIA, drivers and teams over the next weeks about nailing the final details of the revisions, but they will be focused on three key areas of the track.

The first idea is to widen and alter the approach to the Turn 5/6 chicane, so it will better allow cars to contest positions there.

As was proven over the Madrid weekend, the curved entry and layout of the kerbing there meant that there was not enough room for two cars to go cleanly side-by-side there.

That meant it was easy to defend and the only real way to get through was to go super aggressive and risk pushing a rival off.

The second area being looked at is the profile of Turn 13, which is the left-hander straight after La Monumental.

This is currently a medium-speed corner, which does not have the level of braking that offers much chance for a car to make a move if they have picked up a tow through the banked corner.

This bend can be tightened a lot to allow cars to fight for position here.

The third area being looked at is widening the track around Turn 20.

This is one of the tightest corners on the track with the barriers currently acting as a narrow pinch point.

The idea here will be to reprofile the entry and barrier alignment to allow cars to make a passing attempt without fear of not making the exit.

The Race has learned that revisions in these three areas had already been proposed to the FIA ahead of this year's race because of concerns that passing would be too difficult.

However, due to the complexities involved in track simulations and the time it takes to go through homologation processes, it was decided that it would make more sense to wait until 2027 to do this.

The timetable to build the track was already quite tight, with work only having started in April 2025, and things had not been helped by a very wet winter in Madrid, which had delayed construction efforts.

It was agreed in the end that it was better to not risk homologation delays potentially hindering construction that would then open the door for much bigger issues if the track was not ready in time.

F1 tracks have to go through detailed approval processes with the FIA in order to be homologated, and Madrid faced extra challenges because those processes also involved local authorities.

Design decisions required dealing with public road changes, rail and aviation stakeholders, emergency officials plus water, draining and other environmental agencies.

The design of the Turn 5/6 chicane was also made more complicated by the tunnel on the exit, which restricts the angle of attack plus the speed at which cars can arrive due to the limited runoff area.

Small changes, significant difference

F1 drivers were in agreement after the race that the Madring circuit needed only one clear and obvious overtaking spot.

Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc reckoned that it would not take a lot of tweaking to make passing possible and therefore change the spectacle dramatically.

"It's a great track and honestly I think everybody did a great job with the track as it is, particularly in qualifying," he said.

"But in the race, there are some corners and it doesn't require a big change, I think just a small change or two small changes could change significantly the racing that we have."

The lessons that many of the drivers have learned in their careers is that a good street track only requires a single good overtaking spot to become a hit.

This is no better proved than at the Macau GP which, while featuring a tight and twisty city section where passing is difficult, has a long straight with a tight-but-wide-entry corner - Lisboa - where cars can pass.

Carlos Sainz, who plans to speak to the FIA about potential revisions to Madring, thought that lessons from Macau and the Azerbaijan GP should be taken on board.

"Good street tracks like Baku, Macau tend to have one single overtaking spot with a very long straight," he said.

"I think we just need to have a look where there's the possibility to add that overtaking spot and see if it's feasible."

items.title: Honda replaces its F1 engine development chief
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Honda is replacing the leader of its Formula 1 engine development programme.

In what it called a "planned transition", Tetsushi Kakuda - who has led the development of Honda's 2026 F1 power unit so far - will be replaced by his current assistant leader Yoichiro Fukao from the start of next month.

Like Kakuda, Fukao has been part of the Honda motorsport set-up for over two decades, holding a variety of roles across its F1 and MotoGP programmes.

"Following the introduction of the new regulations in 2026, and with further regulatory changes expected from 2027 onwards, Honda aims to establish a robust development framework and deliver a highly competitive PU by transitioning to the new structure at an early stage," said Honda's statement announcing the change.

Honda and Aston Martin's poor form in their first season together has been one of the biggest storylines of F1 2026.

The partnership is ahead of only newcomer Cadillac in the constructors' standings having scored just three points all season.

Major upgrades to both the chassis and engine either side of the summer break provided some encouragement but have not been truly transformative. Driveability remains a particular concern.

Lance Stroll retired early in Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix while Fernando Alonso struggled to a twice-lapped 17th place, after which he said "the engine was very bad today, the boost control was difficult" - though his pace was also affected by early damage.

Asked in Madrid for his thoughts on the progress with Honda's upgraded engine over the three events since its debut, Aston Martin's chief trackside officer Mike Krack said he accepted that engine gains would be slower than chassis progress.

"We are in this together, we came a long way I think since the start of this collaboration and the progress has been steady," he replied.

"Now the progress for anyone is never quick enough. But we also need to understand that on the chassis side you can make progress quicker than on the power unit side, so that is something we are discussing, we are aware of and, I think, Honda is the first one who would like to be better and everyone else as well.

"We have solved a couple of issues that have been problems before and we will work from there and make progress step by step."

items.title: Grosjean apologises for 'misunderstanding' Brown's Piastri comments
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Ex-Formula 1 driver Romain Grosjean has apologised for how he represented McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown's comments about Oscar Piastri at the Spanish Grand Prix. 

Grosjean was commentating qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix on French TV channel Canal+ when he reflected on comments from Brown on Piastri that Grosjean said left him "speechless". 

That referred to an interview on F1TV's post-qualifying show between Brown and F1TV's four presenters - Laura Winter, Grosjean himself and fellow ex-F1 drivers Juan Pablo Montoya and Jolyon Palmer. 

Asked by Winter for his reaction to Norris taking pole, Brown told them "the whole lap was amazing and Lando's just getting better and better and better.

"When you see a lap like that put down, you just go, ‘he's a world champion'."  

When Montoya asked what Piastri, seventh in qualifying while Norris was fastest, needs to take a step up in qualifying, Brown replied: "I think a) you got Lando on his A-plus game, right? So I don't think there was anything left laptime-wise there. So he found that. 

"Oscar's been right there with him all weekend and just didn't get that same extra lap. We'll continue to look at it. 

"He'll look at the data and probably do what we all did and go, 'wow, what a lap' as well." 

On Sunday, while commentating on the grand prix for Canal+, Grosjean described Brown as taking a chainsaw to Piastri's performance. 

He claimed that when asked about the difference in Norris and Piastri's performances, Brown had said Norris is a world champion and better than Piastri. 

Grosjean's comments quickly gained traction on social media on Sunday, becoming one of the trending topics. 

Then on Sunday night, Grosjean took to social media to apologise and clarify his comments. 

"Today, I made a comment on Canal+ regarding Zak Brown's comments about Oscar Piastri during an interview yesterday on F1TV, which I was part of," Grosjean wrote. 

"I completely misunderstood his words and want to apologise for that. I know how important it is to Zak and the entire McLaren team to respect their drivers and treat them fairly and equally.

"McLaren had the fastest car today and were unlucky with the VSC.

"I'm sure both Lando and Oscar will have another chance to fight for the win in Baku."

items.title: Norris calls out 'unfair' VSC rules after lost Madrid win
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Lando Norris says Formula 1 should change its “unfair” virtual safety car rules that robbed him of victory at the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix.

Norris was looking on course for victory at the Madring before an ill-timed virtual safety car for Lance Stroll’s stricken Aston Martin took it away. 

The McLaren driver had already passed the pit entry when the virtual safety car was called, while those chasing him, like Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen, were able to pit and lose far less time than Norris, who pitted the next lap under green flag conditions. 

“I was just unlucky, I was the only one on the whole grid who doesn’t get a pitstop,” Norris told Sky Sports F1 after the race. 

“So I lose 20 seconds on the whole grid, this is out of my control, it’s out of their control, it’s… It’s a rule that shouldn’t define a race. 

“A race should be won by the guy who can put in the best performance, who maybe takes a risk by going long in a stint, and maybe you get a safety car later on and things can help. 

“You know that’s one of the big factors but for everyone to get a VSC pit and for me to get nothing…It’s just, it’s unfair, but it’s happened in the past, others have won from it, probably won it for me in the past. 

“It’s just…I don’t think many people have lost a race win over it. So it’s frustrating I don’t feel like it’s the way you should lose. 

“We spoke about it in the past in drivers’ briefings, saying they should leave it out at least for a lap, so it’s equal for everyone. 

“Today I was the only one who lost out and I lost about 20 seconds of race time and that’s… that’s not how it should be.” 

Norris added: “It's been brought up many times over the years by different drivers. I think there's always probably some cons to doing it. 

“But it's tough. Like I said, I've won from it in the past. I've lost from it in the past, over the course of a season it's hard to know if it's a good thing or a bad thing. It probably equals out over time.

“It just hurts more the fact I lose a win. There's literally nothing I could do as a driver today to do a better job. Pole, led the race. And to lose it for nothing in my control is... I don't think how a race should be won. 

“I think people, I hope people agree, I think people would agree…but it is racing and it's happened. So I can't really complain about it. I can be upset about it, but I can't really complain about it.”

As well as the idea of leaving out the VSC for a full lap, Norris also floated, “Or you just block the pit entry and no one can box, apart from if you have a puncture or something. 

“So I think there's a few things you could do to make it more simple and more fair for everyone. But that's a bigger discussion. 

“This is not something I can just ask for. I think it's something as a group of drivers, I think we would all want. But there's a lot more to it, depending on if it's raining and there's a VSC and you're on slicks, does it mean you can box or not? So it's a complicated subject.

“But I think as a collection of drivers, if we all talk about it, I think everyone wants the same thing and that's just fairness for everyone. 

“I'm complaining about it today. I could benefit from it next week, next time out and I could win because of it. I have to take it on the chin. But I just hope it doesn't happen to anyone again, because it's just not how you should lose a race.” 

Asked whether he’d like to see a rule change, Verstappen - sat next to Norris in the post-race press conference - said: “I’ve also won races because of it. I've lost races because of it. 

“It is extremely painful today for Lando in that case to lose a win. Like sometimes it can be, you might lose points, but this time it's a win. That's really not nice. 

“But unfortunately, I think a lot of drivers have had it that you win some, you lose some. But can it be better? Probably yes, in the future. But we'll probably talk about it in the next briefing and see if there is anything that can be done.” 

Race winner Antonelli acknowledged Norris “deserved to win” the race. 

Norris’s McLaren team boss Andrea Stella was asked by The Race whether changes needed to be made to the VSC rules.

“Offering a personal opinion, I'm puzzled myself as to what's right,” Stella replied.

“Is it correct to give enough duration such that everyone will have been subject to the same track conditions, so for instance the virtual safety car lasts at least one full lap or you just keep it in the hands of the gods and sometimes you're lucky, sometimes you are not?

“I'm not sure myself but in general there's the right place where is a sort of conversation, which is the Strategy Advisory Committee [SAC] and this is a topic that may be added to the agenda and discussed over there. 

“But if it's a change it will have to be a change that goes through the SAC, then we have confirmation and then we have to do at some stage in the sporting regulations.

“But I would envisage such that this is a relatively lengthy process unless there's a big push from F1, from the institutions, FIA or F1 to say ‘we need to make this different’. 

“As a competitor at the moment, I don’t have a clear idea.” 

Stella made it clear he had no problem with how the Spanish GP race director handled things on Sunday.

Like all the times in which a safety car or a virtual safety car timing or duration has a large influence on a race, we have an opportunity to review whether we can do things differently, but this is not under the jurisdiction of the race director,” Stella explained.

“The race director applies the guidance and the regulations at the moment of the race that he is directing.

“When there's a situation like the one that caused the virtual safety car, the attention of the race director and rightly so, is on when the conditions exist to turn the virtual safety car on and when they exist to turn it off. 

“I don't think he takes a look at what's happening in the race; it would be a big distraction. 

“So I think we have absolutely no comment on the race director themselves. I think they've done a good job according to what is the present. 

“Perhaps there's a wider reflection that the Formula 1 community should apply as to whether to keep things like they are or [if you should] introduce ways of maintaining more fairness, but this is not for the race director to do.”

items.title: 'I almost fell asleep' - drivers react to dull Madring F1 debut
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
The 2026 Spanish Grand Prix  was a procession - but what do Formula 1 drivers think is the main problem with the Madring, and what are their proposed solutions?

The Madring is part new, permanent circuit, and part existing roads that flow in and out of the IFEMA conference centre in the north-east of Madrid. It therefore benefitted from a partial blank slate.

In a recent interview with Architectural Digest, designer Jarno Zaffelli said: "Testing was very positive, so I am quite excited to see what Formula 1 has to say," 

"No other course has this particular character, in my opinion, in terms of its flow.

"I hope it gives the drivers and fans a unique feeling. And I would hope that people walk away recognising that it's possible to build a street circuit that is not boring."

A street that's not boring, at least. The race… a different story.

What the drivers said about Madrid's first race

There was consistent praise over the location and the atmosphere at the Madring with drivers including Fernando Alonso, Carlos Sainz, Lewis Hamilton and Arvid Lindblad among those enthusing over the off-track experience.

But Lindblad did concede that it "wasn't the most exciting race" while Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto was asked whether it was as dull to drive as it was for some watching.

"Yeah, I almost fell asleep as well," replied the Brazilian.

Haas's Esteban Ocon said that a lack of tyre degradation and graining on Sunday made for a boring race.

"It was like 120% from as soon as you pitted to the end. And because the graining didn't happen, that's where we ended up. If we had a race on Friday, it would have been much better."

The track layout itself garnered heavier criticism.

Max Verstappen's lap one off at the opening chicane summed up how little space there was to pass there, while the Turn 5-6 chicane was branded too narrow and the various left-handers after the banked La Monumental gave drivers little room.

"I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes, mint!" said McLaren's Lando Norris in the press conference.

A lot of the corners also offer little visibility, and drivers including Sainz pointed out safety concerns.

"Same as in Jeddah and Baku, it's poor," he said. "But it seems like the FIA is happy to go in this direction moving forward in terms of new circuits, which obviously, as drivers, we are raising our… not concerns - but our point of wanting to keep improving safety.

"We're going to go towards these circuits because going at 260km/h, 270km/h [162-168mph] on esses that you cannot see through is definitely eye-opening and definitely makes you question how safe everything is."

Compatriot Alonso deflated the hype around La Monumental as he said his Aston Martin press officer could have taken the corner flat out.

"It is sad, you know, in a way, with this generation of cars to come to a very nice circuit like this one, with challenges here and there, like Monumental corner, Turn 12, and the driver input is just nothing. 

"Michael [Clayton, press officer] can drive in Turn 12 because you go flat with no deployment," he said.

What solutions have drivers offered?

George Russell touched on a fundamental issue with the track.

"I guess the one small frustration in the design is just the lack of clear overtaking opportunities. On every track, at the end of a long straight, you need a clear opportunity to overtake, and the longest straight here goes into that tight roundabout section. So that's probably the only thing we wish was different."

Norris was forthright, saying: "They should get rid of [Turns] 18-19 - useless."

He explained that the track could be improved with a "straight line from [Turn] 17 straight to 20, have a much wider entry like Austin Turn 1 or Turn 10 in Austin. 

"A big hairpin, you create much better opportunities for everyone and you'll be able to enjoy the race. There's some simple changes and maybe some trickier ones like Turn 5, 6, 7."

Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas said it was "quite easy" to block after the longest straight, echoing Russell's comments. 

He added: "What I'm not a big fan of is the sector two and three, how blind it is, especially people on the slow laps. Sometimes it's a bit sketchy, unnecessarily blind in places. But that was the first time we went to Saudi, it was the same issue and then they widened some of the walls, so I don't know - maybe there's some room for improvement."

Aside from Turns 13 (left-hand kink) and 20 (sharp left-hander), Turn 5 garnered the most criticism as, while it's a heavy braking zone, the entry to the chicane is bumpy, there are high kerbs, and the track is still narrow - essentially ruling it out for overtakes.
